transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, I suppose what brings me in is... I just feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. It’s hard to explain, but it’s like there’s this engine inside me that just won’t idle. I’m a special education teacher, so my days are already pretty packed and chaotic, but I’ll finish up one thing at school—like, say, I just finished grading some modified assignments or writing up an IEP report—and I immediately jump right into the next thing without even taking a breath. I’ll start rearranging the desks, or sorting the supply closet, just... boom, boom, boom, onto the next task. 

And it’s not just at school, it’s at home, too. I get back to the house and I’ll finish fixing a hinge on the kitchen cabinet and instantly pivot to pulling weeds in the garden, and then before I even wash my hands I'm sweeping the garage. I just never seem to be able to shut myself off. You'd think at 58 years old I'd be looking to sit back in my recliner and just watch the evening news or relax for five minutes, but I just can't do it. I'm just constantly, constantly going, and it's exhausting, honestly, but I just don't know where the off switch is.
Have you noticed any periods in your life where your mood was unusually high, euphoric, or irritable, significantly different from how you normally feel?

No, not really... I mean, I don't think so. Euphoric? No, no. I mean, sure, I get happy, you know? Like when one of my kids at school finally grasps a concept we’ve been working on for weeks—like last Tuesday, I have this one student who finally understood how to sequence his picture cards without me prompting him, which was just fantastic, a real breakthrough for him and for me, honestly—but I wouldn’t call that euphoric or some unusually high mood. It’s just normal happiness, just a good day at work. 

And as for irritable... well, my wife sometimes says I get a little snappy when I’m in the middle of a project. Like, just this past weekend I was taking apart the carburetor on the lawnmower because it was sputtering, and I had all the tiny little screws and gaskets laid out on this blue tarp on the driveway, and she came out to ask if I wanted to stop for lunch. I might have barked at her a little bit, but that’s just because I was covered in grease and if I walked away right then I knew I’d lose my train of thought and forget how the linkage went back together. But it’s not like it's some totally different mood state, if that makes sense? It’s not like I wake up one week and I’m suddenly angry at the world, or conversely, feeling like I'm the king of the world. 

My mood is actually pretty steady, day in and day out. It’s really just my body, or my brain’s engine, that’s always revving so high. The mood itself, the actual feelings I have, they stay pretty even-keel. I just have to be doing something constantly, regardless of whether I'm in a good mood or a bad mood. Like yesterday, I was perfectly content, just completely fine and relaxed in my head, but I still spent three straight hours reorganizing the garage shelves alphabetically by hardware type because I just couldn't sit in the house. So, no, no weird mood swings or highs like that. Just the constant moving.
Looking back at your younger years, did you experience this same need to be constantly active and unable to sit still when you were a child or teenager?

Oh, absolutely. Oh my goodness, yes. It's funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my sister about this the other day, actually. We were going through some old boxes of our parents' things—they passed a few years ago, but we’re just now getting around to sorting out the attic, which is a whole other project I’ve thrown myself into—and we found some of my old report cards from elementary school. And let me tell you, the comments from the teachers were almost identical year after year. 

My mother, God rest her soul, she used to joke about it all the time. She'd say that even back in second or third grade, I practically taught the class from my seat. Well, I say "from my seat," but the reality was I was rarely actually *in* my seat. I was always up, wandering over to the pencil sharpener, or leaning across the aisle to see what Johnny was drawing, or just standing up beside my desk for no reason at all. I was a real talker, too. I’d just blurt things out. The teacher would be halfway through explaining the directions for a spelling worksheet, and I’d just cut right in, "Are we supposed to use cursive? Do we write on the back?" I just couldn't hold it in. It was like the thought popped into my head and it had to come out of my mouth that exact millisecond. 

So, yes, this... this engine, this constant need to be doing something or moving or talking, it’s been with me my whole life. It’s definitely not a new development. I know sometimes people get restless when there’s a big life change or something, but for me, this is just how my brain has always operated, long before I was an adult, long before I ever stepped foot into a classroom as a teacher myself. It’s just... me. Always has been. I just used to get in trouble for it a lot more when I was eight than I do at fifty-eight! Though, I suppose my wife might argue that I still get in trouble for it now and then, especially when I start vacuuming the living room at six in the morning on a Saturday because I just couldn't lie in bed a minute longer. But yes, to answer your question, it’s been this way since I was a little boy.
